**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Inference capacity for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two of our internal customers have started quietly routing some workloads to a hosted API, which is exactly the kind of drift that becomes permanent if we don't address it. The question on the table is whether we buy more hardware or get more out of what we already own. I want to make the case that we should do the second first, and that the case is stronger than it might initially appear.

The instinct to buy is understandable. Our utilization numbers look alarming on a dashboard: the cluster sits above 80 percent busy during business hours, and capacity planning heuristics would say we're overdue for expansion. But utilization is a slippery number. When we dug into the scheduling logs, we found that a meaningful fraction of our "busy" time is fragmentation — small requests wedged onto large cards, batch sizes chosen conservatively, models held resident on GPUs that only see traffic a few hours a day, and a nightly batch job that monopolizes capacity in a pattern nobody has questioned since it was written. None of this is waste in the sense of idleness; it's waste in the sense of poor fit. Buying more hardware to relieve that pressure would be like adding lanes to a road whose problem is bad signal timing.

The cost asymmetry matters here. New hardware is a large, lumpy, largely irreversible commitment: capital outlay, rack space, power, cooling, and — less obviously — the operational surface of another generation of cards to keep patched and scheduled around. Once purchased, it anchors our architecture and our budget for years, and it depreciates in a market where accelerator economics shift every few quarters. The alternative — better scheduling, dynamic batching, quantization where quality permits, consolidating rarely-used model replicas, moving the batch job off-peak, and tightening the autoscaling policy that currently over-provisions for worst-case load — costs engineering time we mostly already have. If it works, we've deferred a large capital expense. If it partially works, we've still learned exactly what our true demand curve looks like, which makes any eventual purchase better targeted. That asymmetry — cheap, reversible experiments that generate information before an expensive, hard-to-undo commitment — is the whole argument in miniature.

Latency is the one place where the buy case has real force, and I don't want to understate it. Some of our queue-time pain is structural: certain interactive workloads genuinely need dedicated headroom, and squeezing utilization too aggressively trades tail latency for efficiency in ways users feel immediately. If we push consolidation too hard, we risk converting a capacity problem into a reliability problem, and the reputational cost of flaky internal services is higher than the line-item cost of a GPU. So the right framing isn't "avoid buying" but "buy only what survives contact with genuine optimization." My expectation, based on the fragmentation we've already measured, is that disciplined scheduling recovers the equivalent of one to two cards' worth of capacity. If the honest number after a serious effort turns out to be lower — if demand has simply grown past what this cluster can ever serve — then expansion is justified, and we'll have the data to size it correctly rather than buying on panic.

There's also an opportunity cost on both sides that we should name. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on the evaluation tooling and observability work that would make all future capacity decisions easier. Conversely, engineering time spent on scheduler tuning is time not spent on product work, and I don't want this to become a quarter-long side quest. I'd time-box it: four to six weeks of focused effort, with a defined target — peak queue times back under ten seconds at current demand — and a pre-agreed trigger that if we miss it, the purchase request goes forward with my support.

**Recommendation:** Do not approve the hardware purchase yet. Fund a time-boxed utilization effort first, with explicit latency SLOs as the guardrail, and treat any resulting purchase as a data-driven follow-up rather than a reflex. The cheapest capacity we can buy is the capacity we're already paying for and not using well.

I want to be clear that this is a judgment call under uncertainty, not a certainty. Demand forecasts for the second half are fuzzy, and if a new internal customer lands, the calculus changes quickly. But given what we can measure today, optimizing first is the option that keeps the most doors open — and that, more than any single number, is what I'd optimize for.

Happy to walk through the scheduling logs with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Capital request for additional inference hardware

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet before committing to any hardware purchase. The case for buying more machines is real, but it is not yet proven, and the cheaper, reversible option — squeezing more out of what we own — is one we have not seriously attempted. If utilisation work stalls or the demand curve keeps climbing, we will be in a much stronger position to make a purchase case in ninety days, with real numbers behind it.

**Where we actually stand**

Our four A100 nodes currently run at roughly 38 percent average utilisation, but that headline number hides the real problem: the utilisation is badly shaped. Batch inference jobs during the overnight window push individual nodes above 90 percent, while daytime interactive traffic leaves most of the fleet idle. We are not short of compute in aggregate; we are short of compute at specific hours, and we have never built the scheduling layer to move work around that shape. Every conversation about buying more hardware has been anchored on peak-hour congestion, not on the fleet-wide picture.

**Cost**

A new node is roughly $180k up front, plus power, cooling, colocation, and roughly $2k/month in ongoing operational cost per unit. That is not an impossible number for us, but it is a permanent commitment to a depreciation schedule that will outlive most of the projects currently competing for budget. By contrast, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time: better queueing, time-slicing for the smaller models, batch consolidation, and possibly MIG partitioning so that interactive requests can share a node with batch jobs without interfering. We estimate six to eight engineer-weeks. Even if we only get utilisation from 38 to 55 percent, that is the equivalent of adding nearly two nodes' worth of capacity for a fraction of the cost, and it is capacity we keep regardless of what we later decide to buy.

**Latency**

The honest counterargument is latency. Our p95 interactive response times degrade badly during the afternoon peak, and no amount of clever overnight scheduling fixes the four hours a day when users actually notice. This is the strongest argument for buying. But we should be precise about the cause: our current setup runs interactive and batch workloads with no isolation, so a long batch job can monopolise a node exactly when a user is waiting. Partitioning and priority scheduling should recover most of the peak-hour latency without new metal. If, after that work, p95 is still unacceptable, we will know precisely how much capacity we are short, and the purchase case writes itself.

**Reliability**

There is a reliability dimension that cuts both ways. More nodes means more redundancy — today, a single hardware failure takes out a quarter of our capacity, which is genuinely uncomfortable. But our current fragility is partly a consequence of poor scheduling: because we pack jobs tightly onto specific nodes, we have no slack to absorb a failure. Better utilisation discipline, counterintuitively, can improve resilience by leaving deliberate headroom. Buying a fifth node before we have failover practice would just mean five fragile nodes instead of four.

**Opportunity cost**

The engineering time for the utilisation project is not free, and it competes directly with the model-evaluation workstream the research team has been asking for. That is a real trade, and I do not want to minimise it. But the utilisation work is also the kind of infrastructure that compounds: queueing, partitioning, and observability we build now will make any future fleet — ours or rented — cheaper to run. Hardware we buy now, if the demand forecast is wrong, becomes a sunk cost depreciating in a rack.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive factor for me. A purchase is effectively irreversible at our scale; the utilisation work is fully reversible and produces information either way. If we invest eight weeks and discover our peak demand genuinely exceeds what four well-scheduled nodes can serve, we will have lost little and learned a great deal. If we buy first and the forecast is soft, we have locked in capital and still have the same scheduling problems.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag two unknowns honestly. First, our demand forecast is based on three months of growth that may not extrapolate; if the research team's new project lands, peak load could double within a quarter. Second, MIG partitioning on our specific hardware generation has known throughput overheads we have not benchmarked ourselves. Both uncertainties argue for the same conclusion: gather the data before the commitment.

**Proposed next step**

Begin the utilisation workstream immediately, with a checkpoint in eight weeks. If p95 latency at peak remains above our target after scheduling improvements, we bring a purchase proposal to this group with measured numbers rather than projections. I am happy to walk through the utilisation data in detail at Thursday's sync.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering team
**From:** Infra planning
**Re:** Inference capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We are at roughly 70% sustained utilization on our local GPU fleet, with peak periods pushing our two oldest nodes past 90% and causing queue delays that users have started to notice. The question on the table is whether to purchase two additional GPU nodes (approximately $85K capital, plus roughly $9K/year in power, cooling, and maintenance) or to invest engineering time in raising utilization on the hardware we already own. My recommendation is that we spend the next six weeks on utilization work before committing to any purchase, with a pre-agreed trigger: if we cannot get sustained utilization above 85% without degrading p95 latency beyond 400ms, we proceed with the purchase immediately after that review.

**Why utilization first**

The case for buying is real and I don't want to minimize it. Our latency tail is degrading during peak hours, and there is a plausible argument that every week of degraded experience costs us goodwill we can't easily measure. But the case for better utilization is stronger on almost every axis we care about.

Start with cost. The $85K purchase is not just capital; it is an opportunity cost. That same budget is currently the leading candidate to fund the data pipeline rewrite we've deferred twice, and the two projects are effectively competing for the same envelope. Utilization work, by contrast, costs roughly three to four engineer-weeks — real money, but an order of magnitude less, and it comes out of time we would partly spend anyway on the batching improvements already on our roadmap.

Then there's the technical reality of where our waste is. Our telemetry from the last quarter shows three concrete inefficiencies: batch sizes are conservative because we never revisited them after the model swap in March; our autoscaling floor keeps two nodes warm overnight when overnight traffic is under 15% of peak; and roughly a fifth of requests are small, latency-insensitive jobs that could be routed to a cheaper queue on the older hardware instead of competing with interactive traffic. None of these are exotic fixes. If they deliver even half of what the telemetry suggests, we buy ourselves the equivalent of one new node for the cost of a sprint. If they deliver everything, we may not need the purchase at all this year.

**Reliability and latency, honestly weighed**

The strongest argument against squeezing utilization is reliability. Running hardware at 90%+ sustained load leaves little headroom for spikes, and a fleet with no slack fails ugly — one noisy job or a traffic burst and queues balloon. This is why I'm proposing 85% as the target rather than 95%. We should treat the remaining headroom as a deliberate reliability buffer, not waste to be eliminated. Similarly, larger batches improve throughput but add per-request latency; we need to tune against p95, not average throughput, and accept that some theoretical capacity is not worth claiming if it costs users 200 extra milliseconds.

There is also a failure-mode asymmetry worth naming. If we buy hardware and it turns out we didn't need it, we've spent $85K on machines that idle — and idle GPUs still depreciate, consume power, and occupy rack space. If we attempt utilization work and it falls short, we've lost six weeks and can still buy the hardware. The downside of trying first is small and bounded; the downside of buying first is not.

**Reversibility**

The purchase is largely irreversible. Hardware depreciates quickly, resale is a hassle, and once the budget is committed to capacity, redirecting it to the pipeline project mid-year will be politically difficult. The utilization work is fully reversible in the sense that it leaves every option open: if it succeeds, we defer or shrink the purchase; if it fails, we buy with better data and probably a better-negotiated configuration, because we'll know precisely what workload profile we need to cover.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about what we don't know. Our traffic forecast for the autumn is soft — the growth projection that motivates urgency comes from the product team and has historically been optimistic by 30–40%. Conversely, there's a risk the utilization gains are illusory: telemetry can mislead, and the small-job rerouting depends on workload mix staying stable. The six-week review exists precisely to replace these guesses with measurements.

**Next steps**

I'll take a proposal for the utilization sprint to Thursday's planning meeting, with the purchase decision scheduled for the review at the end of it. Comments welcome before Wednesday EOD.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own before committing to any new purchases. This is not a claim that we have enough capacity forever; it is a claim about sequencing, information, and reversibility. The utilisation work is cheap, fast, and informative, while the purchase is expensive, slow, and largely irreversible. Doing the former first makes the latter decision better, whichever way it eventually goes.

**Where we actually stand**

Our current fleet runs at roughly 35–40% utilisation on weekdays and drops sharply on evenings and weekends. That number is not an indictment of anyone; it is the natural result of how the hardware was allocated — project by project, at moments of peak optimism, with each team holding a buffer against the risk of being caught short. But the aggregate effect is that we own, in effect, one and a half to two clusters' worth of capacity while using the equivalent of one. The gap between those two numbers is where this memo lives.

**The case for buying**

The argument for new hardware is straightforward and not wrong. Latency on our shared queue has crept up, and teams feel it. When a researcher waits six hours for a job that takes forty minutes to run, the real cost is not the electricity — it is the experiment they didn't bother to run, the idea they shelved because iteration was too slow. Opportunity cost of this kind doesn't show up on any invoice, and it is the strongest card the purchase argument holds. There is also a genuine reliability concern: we have no meaningful redundancy, and a single hardware failure in one pool can stall a project for days. More machines would buy resilience as well as throughput.

**The case against buying now**

But the purchase path has problems that the utilisation path does not. First, cost: at current prices, a meaningful expansion would consume most of our capital budget for the year, and hardware depreciates quickly. We would be making a large, one-way bet on our own demand forecast — a forecast that, if we are honest, has been wrong in both directions before. Second, irreversibility: once bought, GPUs are hard to sell at anything close to what we paid, and they lock us into a power and cooling envelope that constrains future choices. Third, and most importantly, buying now would tell us nothing. If we purchase while running at 38% utilisation, we will never learn whether the shortage was real or manufactured by our own scheduling habits.

**What utilisation work actually looks like**

The alternative is not doing nothing. It is a focused effort over the next eight to ten weeks: consolidating fragmented reservations, building a shared queue with real priorities instead of informal ones, enabling job packing so small workloads share large cards, and measuring everything. Some of this is unglamorous plumbing. Some of it is social — teams will need to give up private buffers in exchange for confidence in the shared pool, and that trade only works if the queue is visibly fair. We should also invest in better failure handling and checkpointing, which addresses the reliability concern partially and cheaply, since a job that resumes gracefully after a crash is worth more than a redundant machine it never needed.

**What this buys us**

If utilisation reaches 65–70%, we effectively add half a cluster's worth of capacity at a fraction of the cost of buying it, and we learn something crucial: what our true baseline demand is. If, after this work, queues are still long and teams are still blocked, we will have a far stronger case — with real data behind it — for the purchase, and we will know precisely what size and shape of purchase makes sense. If demand turns out to be softer than we thought, we will have saved a large sum and preserved our flexibility.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about the risks of this recommendation. Utilisation efforts can fail for organisational rather than technical reasons, and if the shared queue becomes a political battleground, we will have spent a quarter and gained little. There is also a real chance that demand spikes mid-quarter for reasons we can't schedule around, and we find ourselves genuinely constrained while the utilisation work is still in flight. To hedge, I propose we identify a modest contingency purchase — perhaps a quarter of the originally proposed expansion — that we can trigger quickly if the data justifies it, rather than committing to the full amount now.

**Decision requested**

Endorse the utilisation-first plan, with a checkpoint review in ten weeks and a pre-approved contingency option. The hardware will still be for sale then; our capital, once spent, will not come back as easily.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on Q3 compute capacity decision

**Summary**

We have been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local GPU hardware, or investing engineering time to raise utilisation of the fleet we already own. After several weeks of measurement and discussion, our recommendation is to invest in utilisation first, and defer the purchase decision by one quarter. The reasoning below is not that buying hardware is wrong in principle — it may well be right eventually — but that we do not yet know enough to buy well, and the cheapest way to find out is to fix what we can measure.

**What the data says**

Our fleet currently averages somewhere between 30 and 40 percent utilisation, depending on how we count. That number is itself uncertain: our accounting differs depending on whether we measure by allocated memory, by SM occupancy, or by wall-clock time with a job resident. Under the most generous definition, we are leaving more than half of our paid-for capacity idle at any given moment. The causes are familiar: long-running notebooks holding memory overnight, batch jobs sized for peak rather than typical load, models kept resident "in case," and a scheduling policy that assigns GPUs statically rather than from a shared pool. None of these are exotic problems. They are the ordinary entropy of a small team that grew faster than its tooling.

**Cost**

The purchase option is not merely the sticker price of the machines. It carries colocation or rack space, power, cooling, maintenance contracts, and — less visibly — the ongoing operational burden of managing more devices. For a team our size, every additional node is a permanent tax on attention. Improving utilisation, by contrast, costs engineering time we would largely spend anyway: better queueing, memory-aware scheduling, aggressive eviction of idle sessions, and honest capacity reporting. The asymmetry is stark. One path spends capital and creates recurring obligations; the other spends time we mostly already budget and produces tooling that compounds.

**Latency**

The strongest argument for buying more hardware is queue latency: researchers wait, sometimes hours, for a free GPU, and waiting is a real cost in lost momentum and context-switching. We take this seriously. But our own traces suggest that most of the waiting is not caused by genuine scarcity. It is caused by hoarding — jobs that reserve capacity they rarely use, and interactive sessions that persist far beyond active work. If that diagnosis is right, better scheduling recovers most of the latency benefit of new hardware at a fraction of the cost. If it is wrong, and we find that even at high utilisation the queues remain painful, that is precisely the evidence we would need to justify the purchase with confidence.

**Reliability**

There is a counterintuitive reliability argument in both directions. More hardware means more redundancy and less contention during failures. But it also means more failure surface, more drivers and firmware to keep in sync, and more heterogeneity to reason about when something breaks at 2 a.m. A smaller, better-utilised, better-monitored fleet is in many ways easier to keep healthy, provided we resist the temptation to run it at 95 percent and leave ourselves no headroom. We should target a utilisation ceiling well below saturation — high enough to be efficient, low enough to absorb spikes and failures.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The purchase is largely irreversible. Hardware depreciates, consumes space and power whether used or not, and locks us into an architecture at a moment when the model landscape is shifting quickly. The utilisation investment is reversible and, more importantly, informative: it produces data, tooling, and habits that remain valuable whichever way we eventually go. Buying now would also spend the very engineering attention that the utilisation work requires — an opportunity cost that is easy to overlook because it hides in people's calendars rather than in a purchase order.

**Recommendation and uncertainty**

We recommend a one-quarter utilisation push: shared scheduling, idle reclamation, and honest per-team accounting, with a pre-agreed trigger — if p95 queue wait remains above an agreed threshold at sustained high utilisation, we proceed to purchase without relitigating the question. We acknowledge real uncertainty in our utilisation numbers and in how much of the queue pain is hoarding versus genuine demand growth. If demand is genuinely growing faster than we can reclaim, the purchase case strengthens quickly, and we should not let thrift become its own form of delay. But we should spend a quarter finding out before we spend the capital.
